name: Fractional CTO / CIO
label: Fractional Engagement
title: Fractional CTO / CIO — Neil Catton
description: Senior technology leadership for organisations that need it — without the full-time appointment. One to three days a week, UK-based, remote or on-site.
standfirst: Senior technology leadership for organisations that need it — without the full-time appointment.

sections.heading: When you need this
sections.html:
The product is in production and the company is growing, but technology decisions keep landing on the desk of someone not equipped to own them. An investor is asking who is accountable for technology before the next round closes. Or the engineering team is delivering, and no one is translating between what they are building and what the board needs to decide.

These are not engineering problems. They are leadership gaps — and they do not require a full-time executive to close.

sections.heading: The engagement
sections.html: One to three days a week, in a regular monthly rhythm. A presence on the leadership team, not a contractor at the edge of it. Owning the decisions a CTO owns — architecture, vendors, risk posture, the shape and hiring of the engineering team — and reporting to the board in language the board can act on.

sections.heading: What you receive
sections.html: A named senior leader accountable for technology. A technology strategy the executive team can own and communicate. Board reporting that says what is true, what it costs, and what is being decided. Decisions made and documented — not deferred until a permanent hire arrives. And when the time comes for that hire, a process run by someone who has held the role.

sections.heading: What it changes
sections.html: The board stops asking who owns technology. The CEO stops translating. The cost is a fraction of a full-time executive, and what the organisation can show for it is specific: direction set, risks named, decisions made.

sections.heading: Experience
sections.html: {{years.Words}} years in technology across 20+ sectors, from computer operator to Group CTO. Programme leadership to £1.5bn. A former CISO. Currently holding fractional and advisory appointments across PE-backed, scale-up, and public sector organisations.

sections.heading: Seen in practice
sections.html: Neil sits on the Attending Panel for CTO Grand Rounds — a live session where founders bring a real technical problem to a panel of independent fractional CTOs for review. See the sessions.

faq.q: How much time does a fractional CTO/CIO engagement take?
faq.a: Typically one to three days a week, agreed at the outset and reviewed as the organisation's needs change.

faq.q: Is this remote or on-site?
faq.a: Both — a mix of remote and on-site work, based in the UK.

faq.q: How long does the engagement usually run?
faq.a: Typically three to twelve months, reviewed quarterly rather than fixed in advance.

faq.q: What happens when we're ready to hire a permanent CTO or CIO?
faq.a: The engagement includes running that hiring process when the time comes, handled by someone who has held the role rather than a recruiter working from a job description alone.

faq.q: How is it commercially structured?
faq.a: A monthly retainer, set for the agreed number of days.

name: Non-Executive Director
label: Board Appointment
title: Non-Executive Director — Neil Catton
description: Independent board-level scrutiny of technology, AI risk, and digital change — a non-executive directorship, typically one to two days a month plus committees.
standfirst: Independent board-level scrutiny of technology, AI risk, and digital change.

sections.heading: When you need this
sections.html:
Technology has become material to the board's risk register, but no one at the table can interrogate it independently. AI is being adopted faster than it is being governed. An acquisition, a transformation, or a regulatory change is approaching, and the board's view of its technology position rests entirely on what the executive team chooses to present.

A board that cannot interrogate its own technology dependencies cannot govern the risks they carry.

sections.heading: The contribution
sections.html: Challenge and support, in that order when it matters. Stress-testing technology assumptions against the commercial thesis. Audit and risk committee input on cyber resilience, data sovereignty, and vendor dependency. Technology scrutiny on acquisitions. AI governance that goes deeper than policy documents. The role is to ensure the board understands the trade-offs it is authorising — not merely the recommendation it is approving.

sections.heading: What the board gains
sections.html: A director who translates technology into commercially legible judgement without simplifying it into uselessness. Questions that change what gets signed. An independent view the executive team respects because it comes from someone who has sat on their side of the table for {{years.words}} years.

sections.heading: What it changes
sections.html: Technology stops arriving at the board as a finished recommendation and starts arriving as a decision the board genuinely makes — with the risks named before they are authorised, not after they have matured.

sections.heading: Experience
sections.html: {{years.Words}} years in technology across 20+ sectors, from computer operator to Group CTO. A former CISO. name: Technology Strategy & Roadmapping
label: Fixed-Scope Engagement
title: Technology Strategy & Roadmapping — Neil Catton
description: A sequenced technology direction the executive team can own, communicate, and deliver. A fixed-scope review, typically four to six weeks, fixed fee.
standfirst: A sequenced technology direction the executive team can own, communicate, and deliver.

sections.heading: When you need this
sections.html: The organisation has technology decisions to make and no shared view of the sequence. Everyone agrees something needs to happen, but not what, in what order, or why now rather than later. Investment cases compete without a common frame to test them against. Or a strategy already exists, written by a vendor with something to sell, and nobody in the room fully believes it.

sections.heading: The engagement
sections.html: A structured review of the current estate, the commercial priorities driving it, and the constraints — budget, skills, timeline — that will actually shape delivery. Working sessions with the executive team to test assumptions and surface disagreement early, rather than let it surface later as delay. The output is a sequenced roadmap: what happens first, why, and what depends on what.

sections.heading: What you receive
sections.html: A written strategy the executive team can present to the board in their own words. A prioritised roadmap with dependencies made explicit, not buried in an appendix. Business cases stress-tested for the trade-offs they actually contain, not just the totals on a spreadsheet. A common frame the organisation can keep using once the engagement ends.

sections.heading: What it changes
sections.html: Technology investment decisions get made against a shared view rather than the loudest voice in the room. The roadmap survives contact with the next budget cycle because the constraints were already built into it.

sections.heading: Experience
sections.html: {{years.Words}} years in technology across 20+ sectors, from computer operator to Group CTO. Technology strategy and roadmapping for organisations from scale-up to public sector, grounded in commercial reality rather than architectural idealism.

faq.q: How long does the review take?
faq.a: Typically four to six weeks, run as a fixed-scope engagement rather than an open-ended retainer.

faq.q: What do we actually receive at the end?
faq.a: A written strategy the executive team can present to the board in its own words, a prioritised roadmap with dependencies made explicit, and business cases stress-tested for the trade-offs they actually contain.

faq.q: How is this different from a strategy a vendor writes for us?
faq.a: A vendor-written strategy usually has something to sell behind it. This is independent — no platform, licence, or delivery contract depends on the recommendation, so the sequencing reflects what the organisation actually needs rather than what closes a deal.

faq.q: How is it commercially structured?
faq.a: A fixed fee, agreed before the work starts, not a day rate that runs open-ended.

faq.q: What happens after the roadmap is delivered?
faq.a: It's built to be used without further involvement — a common frame the organisation can keep using once the engagement ends. Some clients bring Neil back for a later review; most don't need to.

sections.html:
AI is on the board agenda because it is everywhere else. Most boards in this position are offered a vendor's view or a consultancy's framework. Neither tells the board what it is actually authorising.

sections.heading: What it changes

sections.html: A deal is moving and technology is material to it. The target's claims — about the platform, the team, the roadmap — need testing by someone who has built and run what is being described. Or the acquisition has completed, the reality differs from the data room, and someone needs to size the gap before it sizes itself.

sections.heading: The engagement
sections.html: Pre-close or post-acquisition. Data room review, management interviews, and the systems themselves where access allows. Assessment of architecture, engineering team, delivery capability, security, technical debt, and what the promised roadmap will actually cost. Turnaround is agreed up front and held — and findings are reported as they emerge, not saved for the final document.

sections.heading: What you receive
sections.html: A written assessment, commercially framed: what is there, what it would cost to fix or to scale, and what that means for the deal. A view on the team — where the knowledge actually sits, and what leaves if certain people do.

sections.heading: What it changes
sections.html: The investment decision rests on evidence rather than the target's narrative. Surprises move from post-completion, where they are losses, to pre-signing, where they are negotiating positions.
